steps.text: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, which makes ATP (the energy supply of the fibre).

steps.text: Myosin filaments lie in the centre of the sarcomere and actin filaments are attached at the ends.

parts.answer: Titin anchors myosin to the Z-line, stores elastic energy and helps the sarcomere recoil, preventing overstretching.

parts.answer: Self-pollination reduces variation; mechanisms preventing it and promoting cross-pollination increase variation; meiosis and gamete fusion make offspring different from the parent.

parts.label: a
parts.approach: A monopolist earns abnormal profit wherever price exceeds average cost at its profit-maximising output, and barriers to entry stop rivals competing that profit away, so it can last into the long run.

steps.text: Define the key terms. A monopoly is a market with a single (or dominant) seller facing the whole market demand curve, so it is a price maker. Abnormal profit is profit above the minimum needed to keep the firm in the industry, which happens when $\text{AR} > \text{AC}$.

Short run: the monopolist maximises profit where $\text{MC} = \text{MR}$. Because the demand (AR) curve slopes downward, MR lies below AR, so the profit-maximising price is read up from that quantity to the demand curve.

Draw a diagram with downward-sloping AR and MR, plus MC and AC curves. Mark $Q_m$ where $\text{MC} = \text{MR}$, the price $P_m$ on the AR curve above it, and the cost $\text{AC}_m$ on the AC curve at $Q_m$.
Because $P_m > \text{AC}_m$, the firm earns abnormal profit per unit. Shade the rectangle with height $P_m - \text{AC}_m$ and width $Q_m$: abnormal profit $= (P_m - \text{AC}_m) \times Q_m$.

Long run: in a competitive market, abnormal profit attracts new entrants, which shifts supply right, lowers price and removes the profit. A monopoly differs because barriers to entry block this process, so the abnormal profit is not competed away.

Explain the barriers that protect the profit: economies of scale or a natural monopoly (a new, smaller entrant cannot match the incumbent's low average cost), legal barriers such as patents, licences and copyrights, control of an essential resource, strong branding and loyalty, and aggressive tactics such as predatory pricing. Link back to the diagram: with entry blocked, demand does not shift left and the shaded profit rectangle persists. A full answer uses the terms correctly and explains the diagram, earning the top band.

parts.answer: Abnormal profit arises in the short run because price exceeds AC at the $\text{MC} = \text{MR}$ output, and persists in the long run because barriers to entry stop new firms eroding it.

parts.label: b
parts.approach: Show why monopoly can be worse than perfect competition on price, output and efficiency, then challenge the word "always" with the cases where monopoly benefits consumers or society.

steps.text: Define monopoly and perfect competition. A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker in a market with many sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and perfect information. A monopolist is the sole seller and a price maker.

The case for the view. Draw side-by-side diagrams. Perfect competition produces where $P = \text{MC}$, which gives allocative efficiency, and in the long run at minimum AC, which gives productive efficiency. The monopolist produces where $\text{MC} = \text{MR}$, so output is lower and price higher, with $P > \text{MC}$: it is allocatively inefficient. Shade the deadweight loss triangle between the monopoly output and the competitive output, lost consumer and producer surplus.

Add the further drawbacks. Monopolists keep abnormal profit through barriers to entry, may lack incentive to cut costs (X-inefficiency) and can use market power to exploit consumers and workers. Use a real example, such as a pharmaceutical firm charging a high price while its patent lasts, or a dominant technology platform with little competition.

The challenge to the view. Economies of scale: a natural monopoly such as water, rail track or electricity distribution may have lower average cost than many small firms, so lower prices are possible. Dynamic efficiency: abnormal profit funds R&D and innovation (pharmaceuticals, technology), whereas perfectly competitive firms earn only normal profit in the long run and have little to reinvest.

Further challenge. Perfect competition is a theoretical benchmark that rarely exists in practice (agricultural markets come closest) and can have drawbacks of its own, such as little product variety, no innovation funds and small firms unable to gain scale. A monopoly is also often regulated (price caps, competition authorities) and is contestable if the threat of entry is real, which limits the harm.

Evaluate and conclude. "Always" is too strong. Monopoly tends to be less desirable on price, output and allocative efficiency, but it can be preferable where economies of scale are large, innovation is vital, or regulation constrains the firm. The judgement depends on the industry, how high the barriers are and how effective regulation is. A top-band answer gives fully explained theory, correct diagrams, developed real-world examples and balanced evaluation reaching a justified conclusion; covering only monopoly's advantages and disadvantages, without comparison to perfect competition, caps the mark at 9.

parts.answer: Monopoly is often less desirable than perfect competition because of higher prices, lower output and deadweight loss, but not always, since economies of scale, innovation and regulation can make it preferable.

parts.label: a
parts.approach: Define deflation, show with an AD/AS diagram how it arises, then explain several distinct problems it causes and why each one harms the economy.

steps.text: Define deflation as a sustained fall in the general price level (a negative inflation rate). Do not confuse it with disinflation, where prices still rise but more slowly.

Cause. Draw an AD/AS diagram. Demand-side deflation: AD shifts left (for example falling consumer confidence or a cut in investment), so the price level and real output both fall. Supply-side deflation: SRAS shifts right (lower costs or productivity gains), so the price level falls while output rises. Label the axes (price level, real GDP) and the shifts.
Deferred consumption and uncertainty. If households expect prices to keep falling they delay purchases, which lowers AD further and creates a downward spiral; lower confidence also cuts investment.
Unemployment and bankruptcies. Falling revenues with sticky wages and fixed costs squeeze profits, so firms cut output and workers, raising cyclical unemployment, and weaker firms go bankrupt.

Real value of debt rises. Fixed money debts become more costly to repay in terms of goods; this hurts borrowers (households, firms, governments), redistributes income from debtors to creditors and cuts spending.

Resource misallocation and policy limits. Falling profits and bankruptcies can waste productive resources, and once interest rates are near zero a central bank has little room to stimulate demand, so deflation is hard to reverse. A top-band answer explains these problems fully with correct terms and a well-explained diagram.

parts.answer: Deflation can cause deferred consumption, uncertainty, higher cyclical unemployment and bankruptcies, a higher real burden of debt, redistribution from debtors to creditors, and policy ineffectiveness.

parts.label: b
parts.approach: Explain how expansionary monetary policy raises AD to close the gap, then weigh its strengths and limitations and compare it with alternatives, ending in a justified judgement.

steps.text: Define terms. Monetary policy is the use of interest rates and the money supply by the central bank to influence AD. A deflationary (recessionary) gap exists when real GDP is below full-employment output, with spare capacity and unemployment.

Explain the mechanism. The central bank cuts its policy interest rate, buys bonds (open market operations or quantitative easing) or lowers reserve requirements. Interest rates fall and the money supply grows, so borrowing, consumption ($C$) and investment ($I$) rise, and a weaker exchange rate may raise net exports. AD shifts right.

Diagram. On an AD/AS diagram, show AD shifting right from $AD_1$ to $AD_2$ along the SRAS curve, raising real GDP from $Y_1$ to the full-employment level $Y_{fe}$, and the price level slightly. The gap is closed. Name the real-world example, such as the US Federal Reserve cutting rates to near zero and using QE after 2008, or the European Central Bank's quantitative easing.
Strengths. Policy can be changed quickly by an independent central bank, shows short time lags in announcement, is flexible, incremental and easily reversed, and does not add to government debt.

Limitations. When interest rates are close to zero there is little room to cut (liquidity trap). If consumer and business confidence is low, firms and households may not borrow even at low rates ("pushing on a string"). Lags still exist before spending responds, effectiveness is weaker with a large gap, and later there is a risk of inflation or asset bubbles.

Alternatives and conclusion. Expansionary fiscal policy (higher government spending or tax cuts) can act directly on AD when monetary policy is exhausted, and supply-side policies help long-run output; many recoveries combine policies. Conclude: monetary policy is effective for modest gaps and when confidence is reasonable, but weak when rates are near zero or the gap is large, so it is best judged alongside fiscal policy. A top-band answer has developed examples, a fully explained diagram and balanced evaluation.

parts.answer: Expansionary monetary policy can close a deflationary gap by raising AD, but it is limited near zero interest rates and when confidence is low, so it is most effective for modest gaps and alongside fiscal policy.

parts.label: a
parts.approach: Treat the two barriers separately, tracing each from cause to its effect on investment, productivity and growth, because covering only one limits the answer to 6 marks.

steps.text: Define terms. Economic growth is an increase in real GDP over time (shown by an outward shift of the PPC or LRAS). Government indebtedness is the stock of public debt a government owes. A poverty cycle (trap) is a self-reinforcing process in which low income leads to low savings and low investment, which keeps income low.
Indebtedness: opportunity cost of debt servicing. Interest payments take government revenue that could fund infrastructure, education and health, so spending on growth-enhancing capital is lower.

Indebtedness: credit and confidence. A heavy debt burden lowers credit ratings and raises the cost of new borrowing. The government may need to raise taxes or cut spending in future, which creates uncertainty and discourages private investment. In extreme cases a debt trap arises where new borrowing only repays old debt.

Poverty cycle: low incomes mean little saving, so there are few funds for investment in physical capital; low spending on health and education keeps human capital and productivity low; low productivity then keeps income low. Describe this loop.

Diagram. Draw a poverty cycle diagram (low income, low savings, low investment, low productivity, back to low income) or show with a PPC or LRAS curve that capital and productivity are not growing, so the curve fails to shift outward.
Link both barriers to growth: lower capital accumulation and lower productivity mean LRAS or the PPC grows slowly. A top-band answer explains both barriers fully with precise terms and a diagram.

parts.answer: Debt servicing, weak credit and uncertainty reduce public and private investment, while the poverty cycle keeps savings, investment and productivity low, so both limit economic growth.

parts.label: b
parts.approach: Explain how market-based policies raise growth and development through efficiency and incentives, then weigh the benefits against drawbacks such as inequality, covering both growth and development.

steps.text: Define terms. Market-based policies rely on markets and private incentives: trade liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, labour market reforms and incentive-related policies such as lower taxes. Economic growth is a rise in real GDP; economic development is a broader improvement in living standards (health, education, equity, poverty reduction).

Explain the effect on growth. Competition and incentives raise efficiency and productivity, attract investment (including FDI) and reduce the cost of production, so LRAS or the PPC shifts outward. Illustrate with an AD/AS or PPC diagram.

Real-world example. For instance, India's 1991 liberalisation and privatisation raised growth rates, or China's market reforms from 1978 or Chile's market reforms. Develop it with specifics on growth, investment and poverty outcomes.

Effects on development. Higher growth can create jobs and raise incomes, helping poverty reduction, and the policies place no burden on the government budget. Without growth, though, development gains are limited.

Drawbacks. Market-based policies may widen income inequality (draw a Lorenz curve moving away from the line of equality), harm vulnerable workers, produce externalities such as environmental damage, take time to work and meet opposition from vested interests. Privatised or deregulated sectors may serve profitable customers only, leaving poorer groups behind.

Alternatives and judgement. Interventionist policies (public investment in infrastructure, education, welfare) address market failure and equity directly. Conclude that market-based policies are usually effective for growth but less reliable for development unless paired with government support. A top-band answer covers growth and development, uses developed examples and reaches a balanced justified conclusion; addressing only growth or only development caps the mark at 9.

parts.answer: Market-based policies tend to promote growth through efficiency and incentives, but their effect on development is weaker because of inequality and externalities, so they work best alongside government support.

steps.text: Why it might: labour economies, since workers can specialise and productivity rises, so output per worker rises and average cost falls.
Why it might: technical economies, because a large firm can afford advanced capital equipment, or buying economies, because bulk purchases earn discounts.
Why it might not: a very large firm is harder to control and decisions can be slower.
Why it might not: communication problems and poorer industrial relations can lower productivity, so average cost rises (diseconomies of scale).
Conclude with a judgement: growth is likely to reduce average cost at first, but only up to the point where management problems outweigh the gains.

parts.answer: Average cost is likely to fall through economies of scale up to a point, after which diseconomies may raise it
parts.mistake: Only stating that average cost falls or rises as a firm grows, with no named economy or diseconomy.

parts.label: a
parts.approach: A population pyramid is a chart, so the definition should say what it shows and which two characteristics it splits the population by.

steps.text: A population pyramid is a graph (bar chart) showing the structure of a population.
It shows the number or percentage of people in each age group (1 mark) and how many are male and female (1 mark).

parts.answer: A chart showing a population split by age and by gender

parts.label: b
parts.approach: Name what changes, then say how that widens the gap between rich and poor; naming the change earns the identification mark and the effect earns the explanation mark.

steps.text: Reason 1: a rise in unemployment.
Explanation: people who lose their jobs are likely to see their income fall, while those in work keep theirs, so the gap widens.
Reason 2: a rise in profits (or interest rates).
Explanation: entrepreneurs and people with high savings gain more income, so the rich pull further ahead of the poor.

parts.answer: Any two of: rise in unemployment, illness, profits, interest rates, regressive taxation, discrimination, unequal education, or economic growth benefiting skilled workers more, each with its effect on the gap
parts.mistake: Giving a cause with no direction of change, such as just "tax", which caps the answer at two marks.

parts.label: c
parts.approach: Elasticity depends on how easily consumers can respond to a price change, so pick influences and follow each one through to the effect on demand.

steps.text: Substitutes: sandals and boots are substitutes for shoes, so if the price of shoes rises consumers can switch.
The closer the substitutes are in price and use, the more elastic demand is. Demand for a particular brand of shoe is more elastic than for shoes as a whole.
Proportion of income: if shoes take a small share of income, a price change has little effect on demand, so demand is more inelastic.
Necessity or luxury: shoes are generally seen as a necessity, which makes demand more inelastic.
Ability to delay and durability: it may not be possible to put off buying shoes when they are needed, which makes demand inelastic; and the more durable the shoes, the more inelastic demand is.

parts.answer: Demand depends on availability of close substitutes, share of income, necessity or luxury, whether the purchase can be delayed and durability

parts.label: d
parts.approach: This is marked by levels, so give developed arguments on both sides, use the economics terms, and finish with a judgement.

steps.text: Define a mixed economic system as one where the private sector and the government both produce goods and services and make decisions.
For: the government can provide public goods such as roads and defence, which private firms would not supply, and can provide merit goods and discourage demerit goods, which improves welfare.

For: the government can redistribute income through progressive taxes and state benefits, and keep unemployment low, which helps the poor, while the private sector generates high incomes and lower prices through competition.
Against: there may still be market failure in the private sector, and high taxation to pay for state spending may discourage enterprise or reduce the incomes of the rich.
Against: state-owned enterprises may be inefficient and the public sector may offer less choice.
Conclude with a judgement that weighs both sides, for example that a mixed system benefits most people if the government intervenes only where markets fail and keeps taxes and state firms efficient.

parts.answer: A mixed system is likely to benefit most people, provided government intervention is targeted and efficient, because it corrects market failure while keeping the incentives of the private sector

parts.label: a
parts.approach: The reward to each factor of production has its own name: land earns rent and capital earns interest.

steps.text: Capital is rewarded with interest.
Land is rewarded with rent.

parts.answer: Interest (capital) and rent (land)

parts.label: b
parts.approach: Enterprise is the willingness and ability to take risks and organise production, so look for causes that reduce the incentive or the supply of potential entrepreneurs.

steps.text: Cause 1: a fall in profits, or a rise in corporation tax or in interest rates on borrowing.
Explanation: this reduces the financial reward from starting a business, so fewer people choose to become entrepreneurs.
Cause 2: a reduction in education, or a fall in population through lower immigration.
Explanation: fewer people have the skills to run a business, or there are fewer people who could become entrepreneurs.

parts.answer: Any two of: lower profits or higher taxes and interest rates, less education, less immigration or smaller population, entrepreneurs moving abroad, recession or war, more regulation, nationalisation, each with its effect on entrepreneurs
parts.mistake: Naming a cause with no direction of change, which caps the answer at two marks.

parts.label: c
parts.approach: Conditions of supply are the factors that change a firm's costs, so identify a change, link it to cost or supply, and finish with the effect on price.

steps.text: Higher costs of production, such as wages, raw materials or tariffs, reduce supply, so the firm raises its price to maintain profit.
A natural disaster or poor weather can create a shortage, which raises price, while good weather can create a surplus, which lowers it.
An increase in indirect tax means the firm may pass it on to consumers as a higher price, especially if demand is inelastic.
Subsidies, new raw material sources, new technology or better training lower costs of production, so the firm can supply more at a lower price.

parts.answer: Changes in costs, weather, taxes, subsidies, technology or productivity shift supply and so raise or lower the firm's price

parts.label: d
parts.approach: This is marked by levels, so develop both sides, use the economics terms, and finish with a judgement.

steps.text: Define a national minimum wage as the lowest legal wage that firms can pay workers.

It might harm: firms that cannot afford higher wages may cut jobs, so unemployment rises. Higher unemployment reduces total demand and output, tax revenue may fall and spending on state benefits may rise.
It might harm: if firms pay higher wages, their costs rise and they may raise prices, causing inflation.
It might not harm: it raises the income of the low-paid and so reduces poverty, and can encourage more people to enter the labour force.

It might not harm: workers who are better paid may be more motivated and productive, firms may train workers to earn a better return, and the minimum may be set below the equilibrium wage so that it has no effect on jobs.
Conclude with a judgement, for example that the harm depends on how high the wage is set relative to the equilibrium wage and on how many firms can afford it.

parts.answer: A rise will not necessarily harm the economy: it depends on how far above the equilibrium wage it is set, because a modest rise helps the low-paid while a large one risks unemployment and inflation
